source.title: Scaling Laws for the Value of Individual Data Points in Machine Learning
source.authors: Ian Covert; Wenlong Ji; Tatsunori B. Hashimoto; James Zou

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses aggregate scaling laws as motivation, but its experiments measure scaling of individual data points’ marginal contributions, not the claim’s aggregate held-out language-model loss, compute allocation, architecture effects, or downstream predictability.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on an adjacent construct: the scaling of an individual training example’s marginal contribution to test loss as dataset size changes. These results do not measure any claim version, so rows are marked versions ["none"]. Aggregate scaling laws in the introduction and related work are background, not results from this study.
record.test_reason: The study measures how an individual training example's expected marginal contribution to test cross-entropy decays with dataset size. It uses small supervised classifiers (logistic regression, 2-layer MLP, SVM) on frozen embeddings and does not vary parameters. It reports no aggregate held-out loss curve versus parameters, tokens or compute. It does not address compute-optimal allocation, architecture shape, or downstream prediction for language models. Aggregate laws (Kaplan, Hoffmann) are cited only as motivation. The construct is adjacent: it uses a power-law-inspired form for per-point contributions. So it does not test any version, and its results belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that per-point marginal contributions decay log-linearly with dataset size, with heterogeneous exponents. They say these laws can be fit efficiently (likelihood and amortized estimators), extrapolate to larger sizes, and aid data valuation and size-dependent point selection. They also note the setting is limited to small models and datasets.
record.recipe_differences: Studies supervised-learning marginal contributions of individual data points across dataset sizes, using logistic regression, MLPs, and SVMs on tabular, image, and text datasets. It does not reproduce aggregate language-model parameter/token/compute scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted individual scaling parameters vary across data points, datasets, and model classes. The authors report deviations for some points and worsening extrapolation R² at larger cardinalities.

fits_no_version.finding: Expected marginal contribution of individual data points follows log-linear decay in dataset size. Overall R² is 0.929–0.993 across 3 datasets × 3 model classes (Table 1) and 0.987 for IMDB logistic regression (Fig. 1). Exponents α(z) are heterogeneous, mode 1–1.5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A training example's expected marginal contribution to test loss decays approximately as c(z)/k^α(z) in preceding dataset size, with point-specific exponents.

fits_no_version.finding: Fitted on k∈[100,1000], per-point predictions keep high Pearson and Spearman correlation up to about 10× larger k. R² degrades beyond the fit range because predictions shrink too slowly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Extrapolation of individualized contribution scaling laws holds for ranking but degrades in absolute accuracy beyond the fit range.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235, 2024
record.problems: The experiments use relatively simple models and small-scale datasets, not large-scale language models. They measure individual marginal contributions rather than aggregate held-out pretraining loss. Some individual points fit poorly, and extrapolation R² degrades at larger cardinalities.
record.rows_left_out: Did not include data-valuation and point-addition application results (Tables 3–8 and Appendix C.3–C.4), because those report application performance rather than a direct measurement of the scaling behavior relevant to the claim. Did not extract numerical values from histogram figures where the text did not give them.

untested.parts: Aggregate held-out pretraining loss versus parameters/tokens/compute; model size is never varied and aggregate loss vs dataset size is not reported.
Extrapolation of aggregate loss fits to larger runs (only per-point contribution extrapolation is tested).
Depth/width/shape effects at fixed parameter count.
Aggregate power-law loss in other modalities or regimes; the image/text datasets here measure per-point contributions, not aggregate loss scaling.
Downstream task performance versus scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of aggregate exponents or compute-optimal split on setup or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: Row values check against Table 1 and the text. For r11, the text says R² drops beyond k=2500 in Section 4.2, and Appendix C.2 says it degrades once k exceeds 1000. Both should be cited. The record's rows_left_out of the Tables 3–8 application results is reasonable. The study's construct is per-example data value, not aggregate model loss, so no version verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Aggregate held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute in language models.
Extrapolation of aggregate loss predictions from small to much larger language-model runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as a function of compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The same aggregate power law across other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream-task performance scaling or prediction from pretraining loss.
Setup and fitting dependence of the aggregate language-model exponents or compute-optimal allocation.

rows.subject: Logistic Regression
rows.operation_detail: Estimate expected individual-data-point marginal contributions at 10 log-spaced dataset cardinalities and fit linear trends in log space.
rows.measure: Overall R² across data points and cardinalities for the initial individualized scaling-law visualization.
rows.note: The experiment uses 1000 data points and averages 1000 sampled contributions per point and cardinality. This R² concerns individual marginal contributions, not aggregate loss.

rows.subject: Logistic Regression
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate individualized scaling-law predictions beyond the cardinalities used to fit them.

conditions.value: up to an order of magnitude larger than the fit range

rows.measure: Prediction accuracy for expected individual-data-point marginal contributions, assessed with R², Pearson correlation, and rank correlation.
rows.value: The R² score drops beyond k = 2500; Pearson and rank correlations remain high, including at cardinalities up to an order of magnitude larger than the fit range.
rows.note: The paper attributes the worsening R² to predictions not shrinking as quickly as empirical contributions.
